eras.title: Early Life
eras.summary: Born into the Mahar community in the Mhow cantonment, Bhimrao grew up under the daily humiliations of untouchability, yet his father's belief in education set the course of his life.

eras.title: Education Abroad
eras.summary: From Elphinstone College to Columbia University, the London School of Economics and Gray's Inn, Ambedkar earned degrees few Indians of any caste held, and began the economic and historical writing that defined his method.

eras.title: Struggle & Activism
eras.summary: Mahad, the burning of the Manusmriti, Kalaram temple, the Round Table Conferences, the Poona Pact, Annihilation of Caste, the Independent Labour Party and the Scheduled Castes Federation: two decades of relentless organisation.

eras.title: Architect of the Constitution
eras.summary: As Chairman of the Drafting Committee and India's first Law Minister, he steered the Constitution through the Assembly, then resigned over the Hindu Code Bill.

eras.title: The Buddhist Turn
eras.summary: The last years: the Buddha and His Dhamma, Deekshabhoomi, and the mass conversion of 14 October 1956 that revived Buddhism in the land of its birth.

eras.title: Legacy
eras.summary: Bharat Ratna, Chaitya Bhoomi, millions at Deekshabhoomi every year, and a living body of thought on caste, democracy and dignity.

events.title: Born in Mhow
events.place: Mhow (now Dr. Ambedkar Nagar), Central Provinces
events.text: Bhimrao Ramji Sakpal is born, the fourteenth and last child of Ramji Maloji Sakpal, a Subedar in the British Indian Army, and Bhimabai. The family belongs to the Mahar community, treated as untouchable in the Hindu social order.

events.title: Loss of his mother
events.text: Bhimabai dies when Bhimrao is about five. His paternal aunt Mirabai helps raise the children after the family moves to Satara following Ramji's retirement.

events.title: Enrols at Satara High School
events.text: Admitted to the government high school at Satara. Untouchable pupils sit apart on a gunny sack they carry themselves, are refused water from the common pot, and are not allowed to touch the blackboard. A Brahmin teacher fond of the boy, Krishnaji Keshav Ambedkar, changes his surname in the school register from Sakpal to Ambedkar.

events.title: Family moves to Bombay
events.text: The family shifts to a one-room tenement in the Improvement Trust chawls at Parel. Bhimrao is admitted to Elphinstone High School, among the first untouchable pupils there.

events.title: Marriage to Ramabai
events.text: At about fifteen, Bhimrao is married to nine-year-old Ramabai (Rami) in a ceremony held in the open shed of Byculla market. Ramabai's quiet endurance during the years of poverty and his long absences abroad is remembered in his dedication of Thoughts on Pakistan to her.

events.title: Passes the Matriculation
events.text: Passing the matriculation examination is so rare for a Mahar boy that the community holds a public felicitation. Krishnaji Arjun Keluskar, a teacher and reformer, presents him with a biography of the Buddha, his first sustained encounter with the Dhamma.

events.title: Joins Elphinstone College
events.text: With a scholarship of twenty-five rupees a month from Sayajirao Gaekwad III, Maharaja of Baroda, arranged through Keluskar, he enters Elphinstone College, University of Bombay.

events.title: Graduates B.A.
events.text: Takes his Bachelor of Arts in Economics and Political Science from Bombay University. His son Yashwant is born in December. He briefly joins the Baroda State service, as the scholarship required.

events.title: Death of Ramji Sakpal
events.text: His father dies. Months later the Maharaja of Baroda, impressed by the young graduate, offers a scholarship of £11.50 a month for three years of study in the United States.

events.title: Sails for Columbia University
events.text: Arrives in New York in July and enrols in the Faculty of Political Science at Columbia University. He lives at Livingston Hall and later Hartley Hall, and for the first time in his life finds that nobody cares what caste he is.

events.title: M.A. from Columbia
events.text: Awarded the Master of Arts for the thesis 'Ancient Indian Commerce'. A year later he completes 'National Dividend of India: A Historic and Analytical Study', later published as The Evolution of Provincial Finance in British India, which earned him the Ph.D. in 1927.

events.title: Reads 'Castes in India' at Columbia
events.text: Presents his first major paper, 'Castes in India: Their Mechanism, Genesis and Development', at Alexander Goldenweiser's anthropology seminar. He argues that caste is 'enclosed class', sustained by endogamy and imitation, not divine ordinance.

events.title: London: LSE and Gray's Inn
events.text: Moves to London, enrols at the London School of Economics for a doctorate and at Gray's Inn to read for the Bar. His influences include Edwin Cannan at LSE and, from Columbia, John Dewey, whose pragmatism shaped his idea of democracy as 'a mode of associated living'.

events.title: Scholarship ends; humiliation in Baroda
events.text: With the Baroda scholarship expiring, he returns to India to serve as Military Secretary to the Maharaja. Peons throw files at him to avoid touching him; no hotel or lodging will keep an untouchable. Within days he leaves Baroda in despair, an episode he later recorded in 'Waiting for a Visa'.

events.title: Professor at Sydenham College
events.text: Appointed Professor of Political Economy at Sydenham College of Commerce and Economics. Students admire him; some caste-Hindu colleagues object to his using the common water jug.

events.title: Testimony to the Southborough Committee
events.text: Gives evidence before the Southborough Committee on franchise, demanding separate electorates and reserved seats for the Depressed Classes. It is his first formal entry into public politics.

events.title: Launches Mooknayak
events.text: Starts the Marathi fortnightly Mooknayak ('Leader of the Voiceless') with help from Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur, who declares at a conference in Mangaon that Ambedkar will one day be a national leader.

events.title: M.Sc. from the LSE
events.text: Back in London on savings and loans, he completes 'Provincial Decentralisation of Imperial Finance in British India' for the M.Sc. (Econ.). He also spends a term at the University of Bonn.

events.title: Called to the Bar; D.Sc. thesis accepted
events.text: Called to the Bar by Gray's Inn and submits 'The Problem of the Rupee: Its Origin and Its Solution' for the D.Sc. (Econ.), awarded in November. The book argues for a gold-exchange standard and later informs the Hilton Young Commission that led to the Reserve Bank of India.

events.title: Founds the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha
events.text: Establishes the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (Society for the Welfare of the Excluded) with the motto 'Educate, Agitate, Organise', to open hostels, libraries and schools for the Depressed Classes.

events.title: Mahad Satyagraha
events.text: Leads thousands to drink water from the Chavdar tank at Mahad, which the municipality had opened to untouchables in law but not in practice. Caste Hindus attack the gathering and later 'purify' the tank with cow dung and curd.

events.title: Starts Bahishkrit Bharat
events.text: Launches the fortnightly Bahishkrit Bharat. In the same year he is nominated to the Bombay Legislative Council, where he serves until 1939.

events.title: Burning of the Manusmriti
events.text: At the second Mahad conference, with the Chavdar tank now under court injunction, the Manusmriti is publicly burned on a pyre built in front of the pandal, a deliberate repudiation of the law-book of caste.

events.title: Evidence before the Simon Commission
events.text: Testifies before the Indian Statutory Commission, which Congress is boycotting, arguing that constitutional reform without safeguards for the Depressed Classes would merely transfer power to the upper castes.

events.title: Kalaram Temple entry satyagraha
events.text: Launches a satyagraha for the right of untouchables to enter the Kalaram temple at Nashik. The campaign continues for five years; the gates do not open. He concludes that the fight is not for temples but for self-respect.

events.title: First Round Table Conference
events.text: Represents the Depressed Classes at the Round Table Conference in London, telling the plenary that the untouchables are 'a fifth of the population' who have gained nothing from British rule and want a government 'of the people, by the people and for the people'.

events.title: First meeting with Gandhi
events.text: Meets Gandhi at Mani Bhavan before the Second Round Table Conference. 'Gandhiji, I have no homeland,' he says. At the Conference in London that autumn the two clash openly over who speaks for the untouchables.

events.title: Communal Award grants separate electorates
events.text: Ramsay MacDonald's Communal Award grants the Depressed Classes separate electorates for twenty years. Gandhi, in Yerwada jail, announces a fast unto death against the provision.

events.title: The Poona Pact
events.text: Under immense pressure to save Gandhi's life, Ambedkar signs the Poona Pact: separate electorates are given up in exchange for 148 reserved seats (instead of 71) in provincial legislatures under a joint electorate. He later wrote that he had been 'placed between the Devil and the deep sea'.

events.title: The Yeola declaration
events.text: At a conference of ten thousand at Yeola, he announces: 'I was born a Hindu, but I will not die a Hindu.' He is appointed Principal of the Government Law College, Bombay, the same year. His wife Ramabai had died on 27 May.

events.title: Annihilation of Caste
events.text: The Jat-Pat Todak Mandal of Lahore cancels its conference rather than let him deliver his presidential address. He prints it himself. Annihilation of Caste argues that caste cannot be reformed without rejecting the sanctity of the shastras, and that 'the real remedy is to destroy the belief in the sanctity of the shastras'.

events.title: Founds the Independent Labour Party
events.text: Launches the Independent Labour Party, bringing together Dalits and workers. In the February 1937 provincial elections it wins 14 of the 15 seats it contests in the Bombay Presidency.

events.title: March of peasants against the Khoti system
events.text: Leads a march of twenty thousand tenant farmers to the Council Hall against the Khoti landlord system in the Konkan, and introduces a bill to abolish it. Later that year he opposes the Industrial Disputes Bill for curbing the right to strike.

events.title: Member of the Defence Advisory Committee
events.text: Appointed to the Viceroy's Defence Advisory Committee during the Second World War, and presses for recruitment of Mahars into the army, leading to the raising of the Mahar Regiment.

events.title: Scheduled Castes Federation; Labour Member
events.text: Founds the All-India Scheduled Castes Federation at Nagpur. Two days later, addressing the Depressed Classes Women's Conference, he says he measures a community's progress by the progress of its women. Joins the Viceroy's Executive Council as Labour Member, where he pushes through the eight-hour day, maternity benefit, and the Damodar Valley and Hirakud multipurpose river projects.

events.title: People's Education Society
events.text: Founds the People's Education Society, which opens Siddharth College in Bombay (1946) and Milind College in Aurangabad (1950).

events.title: Who Were the Shudras?
events.text: Publishes Who Were the Shudras?, dedicated to Mahatma Phule, arguing that the Shudras were originally Kshatriyas degraded by Brahmin refusal to perform their upanayana. He is elected to the Constituent Assembly from Bengal with the support of Jogendranath Mandal.

events.title: India's first Law Minister
events.text: Independent India's first Cabinet is sworn in; Nehru invites Ambedkar to be Minister of Law. Re-elected to the Constituent Assembly from Bombay after Partition removed his Bengal seat.

events.title: Chairman of the Drafting Committee
events.text: The Constituent Assembly appoints a seven-member Drafting Committee and elects Ambedkar its Chairman. With other members ill, absent or abroad, much of the burden falls on him; T.T. Krishnamachari later told the Assembly that 'the burden of drafting this Constitution fell on Dr. Ambedkar'.

events.title: Marries Dr. Sharada Kabir
events.text: Marries Dr. Sharada Kabir, a physician from a Saraswat Brahmin family who had treated him for diabetes and neuritis. She takes the name Savita; the community calls her 'Mai'.

events.title: Presents the Draft Constitution
events.text: Moves that the Draft Constitution be taken into consideration. Defends the strong Centre, parliamentary government and the Directive Principles. The clause-by-clause debate lasts a year and takes up 7,635 amendments.

events.title: 'The Grammar of Anarchy'
events.text: In his closing speech he warns that on 26 January 1950 India will enter 'a life of contradictions': equality in politics, inequality in social and economic life. He cautions against hero-worship, against 'the grammar of anarchy', and says that however good a constitution may be, it will prove bad if those who work it are bad.

events.title: The Constitution comes into force
events.text: India becomes a Republic under the Constitution adopted on 26 November 1949. Articles 14, 15, 17 (abolition of untouchability) and 25 carry his imprint; the first issue of the Buddhist journal he supported, and the Buddha image at the Siddharth College, mark the year's other preoccupation.

events.title: World Fellowship of Buddhists, Colombo
events.text: Attends the inaugural conference of the World Fellowship of Buddhists in Ceylon and addresses the Young Men's Buddhist Association on the rise and fall of Buddhism in India.

events.title: Resigns over the Hindu Code Bill
events.text: Resigns from the Cabinet after the Hindu Code Bill, which would have given Hindu women rights of divorce, inheritance and monogamous marriage, is shelved under orthodox pressure. 'To leave inequality between class and class, between sex and sex... and to go on passing legislation relating to economic problems is to make a farce of our Constitution.'

events.title: Elected to the Rajya Sabha
events.text: After losing the Bombay North Lok Sabha seat in the first general election, he is elected to the Rajya Sabha from Bombay State. Columbia University confers an honorary LL.D. in June, citing him as 'one of India's leading citizens, a great social reformer and a valiant upholder of human rights'.

events.title: Honorary D.Litt. from Osmania University
events.text: Osmania University confers an honorary doctorate. Through these years he is writing The Buddha and His Dhamma, Thoughts on Linguistic States, and Riddles in Hinduism.

events.title: World Buddhist Conference, Rangoon
events.text: Attends the third World Fellowship of Buddhists conference in Rangoon; he had already visited Burma for the Sixth Buddhist Council earlier that year. He speaks of his plan to bring the Dhamma back to India.

events.title: Bharatiya Bauddha Mahasabha
events.text: Founds the Bharatiya Bauddha Mahasabha (Buddhist Society of India). In the same month he gives a BBC interview that is now the best-known film record of his voice, and installs a Buddha image at Dehu Road near Poona, announcing that a book on Buddhism is nearly done.

events.title: 'Why I like Buddhism' on the BBC
events.text: In a BBC radio talk broadcast on Buddha Jayanti, he explains his preference for Buddhism: it teaches prajna (understanding), karuna (love) and samata (equality), which 'man requires for a good and happy life'. He completes The Buddha and His Dhamma and writes its preface.

events.title: Conversion at Deekshabhoomi, Nagpur
events.text: On Vijayadashami morning, Ambedkar and Savita take the Three Refuges and Five Precepts from the Burmese monk Mahasthavir Chandramani. He then administers the oath, with his Twenty-two Vows, to a gathering estimated at nearly four hundred thousand, the largest mass religious conversion in modern history. The next day another gathering takes the vows, and on 16 October he repeats the ceremony at Chandrapur.

events.title: 'Why Nagpur?' speech
events.text: In a long address the day after the conversion, he explains why he chose Nagpur: it was the land of the Nag people who had spread the Buddha's teaching, and the choice had nothing to do with provoking anyone. 'This conversion has given me enormous satisfaction and pleasure unimaginable. I feel as if I have been liberated from hell.'

events.title: Last public lecture: 'The Buddha and Karl Marx'
events.text: At the fourth World Fellowship of Buddhists conference in Kathmandu, he delivers his final lecture, comparing the Buddha's path of non-violent social transformation with Marx's. He visits Sarnath and Kushinagar on the way home.

events.title: Mahaparinirvan
events.text: Dies in his sleep at his Delhi residence, days after completing the last chapters of The Buddha and His Dhamma. His body is flown to Bombay; on 7 December an estimated half a million people follow the procession to the Dadar cremation ground, where he is cremated with Buddhist rites. The site becomes Chaitya Bhoomi.

events.title: The Buddha and His Dhamma published
events.text: The People's Education Society publishes his final work posthumously. It presents the Buddha's teaching as a rational, ethical and social gospel, and becomes the foundational text of Navayana Buddhism.

events.title: Deekshabhoomi stupa begun
events.text: Construction begins on the great stupa at Deekshabhoomi, designed by Sheo Dan Mal. Completed in 2001, it is among the largest hollow stupas in the world and draws over a million visitors every Dhammachakra Pravartan Din.

events.title: Writings and Speeches series begins
events.text: The Government of Maharashtra begins publishing Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, edited by Vasant Moon. The series now runs to seventeen volumes and is the standard source for his work.

events.title: Bharat Ratna
events.text: Awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, posthumously, during the birth-centenary year. His portrait is unveiled in the Central Hall of Parliament on 12 April.

events.title: Bust at Columbia University
events.text: A bust of Ambedkar is installed at Lehman Library, Columbia University. In 2004 Columbia names him among its greatest alumni for the 250th anniversary, and in 2023 the Supreme Court of India displayed his Columbia thesis in an exhibition.

events.title: Ambedkar House, London
events.text: The house where he lived as a student in 1921-22 is bought by the Government of Maharashtra and opened as a memorial museum.

events.title: 125th birth anniversary
events.text: The 125th anniversary is marked at the Bhim Janmabhoomi memorial in Mhow and by the United Nations, which hosts its first Ambedkar Jayanti observance on the theme of combating inequalities.

events.title: Seventy years of Dhammachakra Pravartan
events.text: Seventy years after the conversion, millions still gather at Deekshabhoomi each Vijayadashami and Dhammachakra Pravartan Din to take the same Twenty-two Vows. This site is built in his honour on that anniversary.
